article.title: Progressive” Voters
article.author: Paul Kleyman
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. While midterm voters spelled relief “B-L-U-E,” chucking out the bums on their ruddy baboon butts, it didn’t take a day for the middling media to muddle over polling data and declare that “radical” progressives, notably Michigan’s Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, had statistically “underperformed” more moderate Democratic victors. Michigan’s new Governor Jocelyn Benson, for instance, beat her Republican rival by 11%, compared with El-Sayed’s 7% margin, a healthy edge by any other electoral standard. That El-Sayed won so handily, if short of Benson’s margin, was quickly sniffed at by mainstream writers at the New York Times , CNN and other media, portending a Dem dilemma for the 2028 election. Never mind that some media analysts recognized the extraordinary success of leftist winners at all, the established Dems are determined to kick their party’s behinds, while spreading public distrust of their own “socialist” colleagues. The NYT’s chief political analyst, Nate Cohn , discerned only a day after the election, for example, “The country voted for Democrats by 13. We would thus expect Democrats to win in Michigan by 13. El-Sayed won by 7. . . . So that’s a 6 or so point underperformance for El-Sayed in Michigan compared to what you would expect, given what we know about what happened nationwide.” MS NOW’s Rachel Maddow reminded viewers that El-Sayed had remarkably predicted last summer he’d unseat the incumbent by 7%, exactly his margin of victory. Perhaps he accounted for the outright racism and accusations of “radicalism” than the post-election count would suggest to raw-vote counters. Most would figure 7% to be a vote of confidence against all odds, not an underperformance. Related: Aging Isn’t Downhill Slide: Cognitive, Physical Improvement Common Dancing with the Swing Voters The Dems’ performance anxiety takes centrist stage with the swing dancers. To corporate media analysis, doing the Lindy with party-unaffiliated “swing voters” must surely chart a safer campaign strategy for Democrats in 2028, right? The PBS NewsHour’s Tamara Keith commented Nov. 9 , “I have spent a lot of time talking to swing voters, and these voters, they want results. And no one was talking about impeaching Pete Hegseth. They're talking about how they want the prices to come down. They want their lives to get easier. . . . And several of them specifically said, I just don't want two years of investigations and impeachments.” Her policy-specific prescription, evidently based on what researchers would call a “convenience sample” of interview (who were they, where, compared to which independents?) doesn’t align with previous extensive polling. Note The Guardian’s Oct. 30 story , headlined “Government Corruption a Top Issue for US Midterm Voters, Exclusive Poll Finds,” with the drophead, “Harris poll for Guardian finds 76% believe officials care more about self-enrichment than helping everyday Americans.” Keith’s remark under-reports the broader news that American voters want both, a better, fairer system with accountability for government banditry. Yet, the presumed advantage of “moderation” takes an unbidden bow. Nixon vs. Schumer Another Dem-designated underperformer is Florida Democratic Socialist Angie Nixon, who lost to incumbent Ashley Moody, who was appointed by Gov. Ron DeSantis in 2024, to fill the seat left vacant when Marco Rubio became Secretary of State. Nixon’s 48% vote closed the usually far wider electoral gap for the Sunshine State’s Democrats to a squeaky 2.9%. On the New York Times Nov. 4 podcast of “The Daily,” program host Michael Barbaro said of Nixon’s loss, “Inevitably, you have to ask, what is it about that candidate? Why didn’t that Democratic candidate do what the Democratic candidate did in all these other places? They were far more progressive.” More astutely, Salon’s Alex Galbraith reported, “The blame for Nixon’s defeat lies almost solely with national Democrats and their stubborn refusal to back Nixon with either messaging or money.” Galbraith quotes Nixon from a September MS NOW interview, saying, “When I did speak with Sen. Schumer on the phone, it was basically a ‘we will see.’ He’s going to ‘look into it.’” He cited her observation that Schumer and the Dem leadership were also “wary of throwing in behind a Black woman in the South following Kamala Harris’ 2024 loss.” Somehow, Dem centrists’ fail their memory test regarding the former vice-president’s losing after she adopted more progressive positions than President Biden, such as backing labor, actually picketing with one union, enforcing anti-trust laws, and more substantially raising corporate taxes. She then echoed Biden’s insistence on continuing to arm Isreal, in the wake of Gaza’s death and destruction. What exactly defines “moderate” campaigning? Related: Almost Blameless: How Lazy Reporting Plays Into Ageist Political Lies The Over-Performers (“Woke” No More) The locution “underperformed” frowns with disappointment, like a helicopter parent’s scowl at Junior’s underachieving A-minus. CNN’s Aaron Blake, gleefully reported, “We saw many of the more moderate Democratic candidates notch some of the biggest over -performances. . . North Carolina Senator-elect Roy Cooper over-performed [Kamala Harris’ 2024 vote] by 23.2 points. . . . Other biggest over-performances came from candidates with less moderate (and even rather ‘woke’) pasts — but who clearly ran as moderates this time. That includes Senator-elect James Talarico in Texas (25.7 points better than Harris) and Senator-elect Dr. Annie Andrews in South Carolina (21.9 points better).” Blake added, “Also telling: In Maine’s 2nd District, Sen. Bernie Sanders-backed state Auditor Matt Dunlap “over-performed Harris by just 8.1 points and lost.” So, over or under, Dunlap is judged a loser all around? The major-media’s number crunchers seldom account for the fear-and-loathing factor likely to have depressed the progressives’ vote in many places. Not only the GOP’s anti-Arab “terrorist” attacks against Dr. El-Sayed, but also the Dem’s own persistent warnings against progressive “extremism,” which tended to bolster Republican cries against “socialists.” The Michigan public-health physician campaigned largely on such “radical” issues as universal health care, affordable housing, clean water (remember the lead crisis in Flint, MI?), and similarly practical community concerns. Yet the doggedly bluish liberal pundits and politicos persist in the beige notion that avoiding perceived controversies at any cost is a winning strategy. Meanwhile, Angie Nixon announced the day after the election that she was forming the Never Scared PAC . She said in a press briefing that the committee will be "dedicated to building the political and economic power of everyday hardworking people across Florida." Although polling can be an essential tool for discerning the interests and druthers of constituencies, the excessively literal parsing of voter identity, the temptation of treating exit polls like a psychiatrist’s couch in the service of a political framework, fails the tenets of basic psychology—and journalism: to listen, assess and not judge. The NYT’s Cohn rightly stated on ”The Daily” podcast, “ Progressive is a hard word to define. It’s a category that people could use to define anyone from a Democratic Socialist to a mainstream Democrat, like Barack Obama could be called a progressive.” But then Cohn overstepped into muddy of judgmentalism, stating, “But what I’m really talking about here is a narrower group of progressive candidates backed by progressive activists who campaigned against the Democratic Party’s establishment, who wanted the party to move towards the left, who don’t merely support Medicare for All or oppose Israel, which a majority of congressional Democrats do, but are the kind of people who stake their campaigns on the issues that progressive activists care about most. . . . And across the board, these candidates are doing worse than you would expect in this national political environment.” That may be true in this electoral instant, but one might also consider that those previously downgraded as socialist, ethnic, female or all of the above, are the ones on the rise compared with past election. Related: Privateering Our Public Goods What’s Being Underestimated Political bean counting has its value, but mere accounting on the balance sheet of one vote cycle fails to account for a citizen’s strains against hope. Among millions of “red” constituents are ever-struggling farmers and steel-town workers, who’ve been long forgotten by bipartisan legislators when it came to allocating their budgets where their rhetoric was. Like Republicans, “activist” progressives worry about their kids’ futures and retirement years at the kitchen table. More than one commentator has observed that in many other advanced economies, Sen. Bernie Sanders’ “socialist” positions—on universal health care, economic justice, clean air and water, and access to good education and jobs are considered moderate . Political journalists, in particular, are failing to interrogate the judgmental slant of electoral labels sharply enough to sever their reporting from loaded party factionalism. As the Democrats and GOPers presumably compete for the soul of the nation—while also picking intramurally at one another—may victory go to the forthright, the inclusive voices proffering well-structured, appropriately-financed plans built on platforms of integrity and, especially, of caring. Is that political over-reach? Maybe, but only to those who underestimate the power of reasoning and decency that was so collectively evident on Nov. 3.
